Then I transferred and turned the whole speech to rebuking the flight of Cepio, and to lamenting the army again. Thus, he was chafing the pain of those who were mourning their own by his speech, and he was calling back and calling back the minds of the Roman knights, among whom the case was being pleaded then, to the hatred of Q. Cepio, from whom they had been alienated on account of the trials. When I sensed that I had established myself in the possession of the trial and of my own defense, because I had already reconciled the goodwill of the people to me—whose right I had defended even with the conviction of sedition—and I had turned the minds of the judges entirely to our case, either by the calamity of the state, or by the grief and longing of relatives, or by their own hatred toward Cepio, then I began to mix into this genre of vehement and atrocious speech that other genre about which I disputed before, of gentleness and clemency. That I was deciding for my associate, who ought to be in the place of a son to me according to the custom of our ancestors, and for all my own reputation and near fortune, that nothing could happen to me more shameful regarding estimation, nor more bitter regarding pain, than if I, who was thought to have been a savior to men often very strange to me but yet my citizens, had not been able to bring help to my associate. I was begging from the judges that they might concede that to my age, to my honors, to my deeds, if they saw me to have been affected by just and pious pain, especially if they had understood in other cases that I was always advocating everything for the perils of friends, and never for myself. Thus, both that entire defense and the case, which seemed to be placed in art—so that he might speak about the Apuleian law, so that he might explain what it was to diminish the majesty—through which I briefly touched and grazed. By these two parts of speech, one of which has recommendation, the other incitement—which are least polished by the precepts of art—all that case was handled by me then, so that I was both most sharp in renewing the hatred of Cepio, and most gentle in declaring my morals toward my own associates.

v. 5. *Perceived* <note>original: "Percepta"</note>.] Gemblacensis: *Precepts* <note>original: "Pracepta"</note>. He called the returning stars *palinōros* <gloss>returning/back-turning</gloss>, as Aratus did.
v. 8. *With the example showing the way* <note>original: "Exemplo monstrante viam"</note>.] For they handed down these annotations to posterity as examples and *rhuseis pragmatikas* <gloss>practical observations</gloss>. Ptolemy: *because of agreeing with them, as they were assigned back to the degrees by the practical observations held by them*. For he calls them *exemplar births*, which they recorded from observations into tables, as we have already shown from Sextus Empiricus.
v. 10. *And the whole alternating* <note>original: "Et totum alterna"</note>.] If it is not an error, he calls "alternating" that which returns into a circle. But I remember that these three words, *aeterna* <gloss>eternal</gloss>, *alterna* <gloss>alternating</gloss>, and *aetheria* <gloss>ethereal</gloss>, are interchanged among themselves in this author by the fault of copyists. Therefore, it is more consistent with the author's mind that *eternal* should be read. For how often is it read thus?
v. 11. *To discern the changes of the Fates by certain signs* <note>original: "Fatorumque vices certis discernere signis"</note>.] Who would doubt that it should be read *to discurre by signs* <note>original: "discurrere signis"</note>, unless someone who had not noticed the lines above? *Discurrere* crept in from the verse that is eighth from this one.
v. 15. *As if mourning for the lost* <note>original: "Tam velut amißis mærens"</note>.] Literally for the Greeks: "The Egyptians, when they saw the sun descending under Cancer and Capricorn, when it was shortening the days from longer ones, would mourn, fearing that the sun might leave them with too little. And that is the time, which is the year of their solstice." When it began to ascend again and make the days longer, they would then celebrate and wear crowns. These things were without doubt written from the *Octaeteris* <gloss>eight-year cycle</gloss> of Eudoxus. In which Eudoxus began the solstice, from which he started his year of *prytaneis*, from the Ides, at which time the sign of the solstice was completed. But see the second book of our work *On the Amendment of Times* regarding this matter.
v. 17. *Nor with the Sun returned* <note>original: "nec Sole regreſſo"</note>.] Gemblacensis and Bonincontrius: *now with the Sun returned* <note>original: "iam Sole regreſſo"</note>. Which is true.
v. 22. *And unknown new* <note>original: "Ignotuſque nouos"</note>.] Better Gemblacensis: *And motionless new* <note>original: "Immotuſque nouos"</note>. He did not speak of "new" spheres in vain because of Britain, discovered by C. Julius Caesar shortly before his own times, which they called a new world.

# The Hessians from Neuss have good fortune, yet they are quite careless.

<margin></margin>
April
Year
1644.
</margin>
The beginning of April started quite well for the Hessian party from Neuss, which city they have currently transformed into a true fortress with seven bastions. However, because they showed themselves to be overly confident and trusted their fortune too much, fortune dealt them an unexpected blow, thereby demonstrating how little she is to be trusted. This is how it came to pass.

After the aforementioned Hessians scouted that four Lorraine regiments, namely the Life Guard Regiment under Colonel Bellemont on foot, Colonel de Fauge, and Colonel Baltin on horseback, were quartered not far from Merode Castle, and in the village of Merode itself Colonel de Gierecourt on foot and Colonel de Mondragou on horseback, those troops set out from Neuss, Kempen, and Calcar under the escort of Colonel Rabenhaupt at night with 500 cavalry, 300 dragoons, and 400 musketeers. On Sunday, April 1st <note>original: 11. Aprilis; the difference represents the Julian vs. Gregorian calendar</note>, they ambushed the Lorraine headquarters. Despite heavy resistance, Colonel Bellemont and some 200 common Lorraine soldiers remained dead, 160 cavalrymen were captured, along with 200 horses and two pieces of artillery, as well as whatever else was found in the quarters. During the ongoing skirmish, after Colonel Bellemont's death, Colonel de Fauge held his ground for more than half an hour until finally his horse was shot from under him, and he was captured as a result. The Lorraine forces then had to retreat toward Colonel Gierecourt's quarters. When Count Christian of Nassau-Siegen and others meanwhile received news of this, he hurried there with 300 cavalrymen and the Mandesloh Regiment. He quickly gathered the scattered Lorraine troops and attacked the Hessians, who had remained in the field unnecessarily long and were firing from the captured cannons. He encountered them at Ober-Em near the woods, called the Hell, where the real struggle began. Both sides fought manfully until the Hessian party fell into disorder, and about 500 men from both sides remained dead on the spot. In this process, the Lorraine colonels and others previously captured by the Hessians, along with the two recaptured cannons and much other loot, were taken back. ### Wellspring 9, Branch 4

Darius the Mede and Cyrus the King of Persia joined together. Darius the Mede was king in Media, and Cyrus came to the throne in Persia. They united Media and Persia and conquered toward the west, the north, and the south. This is why the text says the ram "pushed westward, northward, and southward" <note>Daniel 8:4</note>. Cyrus and his son after him conquered many lands, as recorded in the history of the Persian kings. Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, sent his generals to conquer the entire East. The reason the East is not mentioned in the ram's pushing is that Persia was already in the East; they did not need to conquer the direction they already occupied. The text says, "no beast could stand before him," meaning the surrounding kings and princes could not withstand the Persian power. The text says he came "from the west" and "on the face of the whole earth," and he "did not touch the ground." This describes the incredible speed of Alexander’s conquests. He did not linger; it was as if he were flying on the clouds of heaven. The he-goat came to the "ram that had two horns" <note>Darius III of Persia</note>. He ran at him in "furious power." This describes the three major battles Alexander fought against Darius, where he eventually destroyed the Persian monarchy and took over the empire. The "notable horn" was Alexander, as Gabriel later explains: "the rough goat is the king of Greece, and the great horn between his eyes is the first king" <note>Daniel 8:21</note>. He is called "notable" because of his fame and his association with the teachings of Aristotle the philosopher; he was a man of great intellect as well as military might. He reached the "ram" and broke his two horns, signifying the total collapse of Median and Persian power. <summary>This page identifies the ram as the Medo-Persian Empire and the he-goat as Alexander the Great, highlighting the speed of Alexander's conquests and his defeat of Darius III.</summary>

# Sāṃkhyasūtravṛttiḥ

The reasoning that "I have pain in my head, I have pleasure in my foot" is used to suggest the all-pervasiveness of the mind; however, the lack of simultaneous perception is due to the sequential movement of the subtle mind. All-pervasiveness is not proven by this. 69

He states another refutation:

Because of the scripture regarding its activity. 70

"Because of its activity" indicates the inference. "Because of the scripture of movement" indicates the text. 70

He addresses the argument that even if it is atomic, it will be eternal due to the absence of a cause:

It is not without parts, because of its combination, like a pot and the like. 71

It is not without parts, it is not without a cause. "Because of its combination"—because of the combination of parts. What is the cause of this? <term>Ahaṅkāra</term> <gloss>ego-principle</gloss>. The fact that atoms have parts is proven by the simultaneous connection with a six-fold [aggregate]. Therefore, the mind is non-eternal, like a pot. 71

He states the division between eternal and non-eternal:

Everything other than <term>prakṛti</term> and <term>puruṣa</term> is non-eternal. 72

This is clear. 72

He addresses the question: how is everything non-eternal, given that time, space, and so on are eternal?

There is no acquisition of parts for that which has parts, because of the scripture that it is without parts. 73

There is no acquisition of a cause for that which has parts—meaning the primordial cause of the world—because of the scriptural statement "Being the root cause, it has no other cause." 73

He refutes the idea that liberation is the manifestation of bliss:

Liberation is not the manifestation of bliss, because it is devoid of qualities. 74

<meta>This page continues Clement’s discussion on the biological and spiritual connection between blood and milk, moving into the symbolic use of milk, honey, and water in Christian initiation.</meta>

## THE INSTRUCTOR, BOOK I

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, the same substance, both blood and milk, serves as a symbol of the Lord’s passion and his teaching. It is permitted for each of us who are infants to boast in the Lord, saying:

->I boast to be of a good father and of such blood.<-
->[To be.]<-

It is already clear that milk is formed from blood through a process of change. However, we can also learn this from looking at flocks of sheep and herds of cattle. During the season of the year we call spring, the atmosphere is more humid. The grass and pastures are full of juice and moisture at that time. The animals first become full of blood, which is shown by the way their veins distend and their vessels become rounded. From this blood, milk flows more abundantly. <margin>B</margin> Conversely, in the summer, the blood is constricted and dried out by the heat. This stops the transformation, and so they produce less milk when they are milked. Furthermore, milk has a very natural kinship with water, just as the spiritual bath <note>original: λουτρὸν (loutron); referring to baptism</note> has a kinship with spiritual nourishment. Those who sip a little cold water with the aforementioned milk find it helpful immediately. The fellowship with water does not allow the milk to turn sour <note>original: ἀποξύνεσθαι (apoxynesthai)</note>. This happens not through some kind of opposition, but through a natural affinity as it ripens. The relationship that the Word <note>original: Λόγος (Logos)</note> has with baptism is the same as the connection milk has with water. Milk is the only liquid that accepts a mixture with water, being received for the purpose of cleansing, just as baptism is received for the forgiveness of sins. <margin>C</margin> It is also naturally mixed with honey, and this again is for cleansing along with sweet nourishment. For when the Word is mixed with love for humanity, he heals our passions and cleanses our sins. The saying:

> ... Speech flowed sweeter than honey,

seems to me to have been spoken about the Word, who is honey. In many places, prophecy raises him above honey and the honeycomb. Furthermore, milk is also mixed with wine.

---

<note>P. 128 in the Potter edition, 107 in the Paris edition.</note>

(44) **Father.** Diomedes says this in Homer, *Iliad* 14, line 113: *I also boast that my birth is from a good father.* (45) **To turn sour.** The Bodleian manuscript reads *epoxynesthai*, but another hand wrote an *a* over the first *e*. (46) **Cleansing.** There is no doubt this should be read as *epi katharsei* (for cleansing) as it appears shortly after. (47) **Honey.** This refers to the custom of the early Christians, who gave those newly baptized a taste of honey and milk mixed together. Clement seems to have alluded to this a little earlier on page 125: *As soon as we are reborn, we are honored with the hope of rest, the Jerusalem above, in which it is written that milk and honey rain down.* Tertullian mentions the same rite in *On the Crown*, chapter 3: *Then, having been received from baptism, we taste a mixture of milk and honey.* In his work *Against Marcion*, book 1, chapter 14, he says that Marcion does not reject the Creator's water with which he washes his own, nor the oil with which he anoints them, nor the fellowship of honey with which he treats them as infants. For infants were once nourished with milk and honey. Barnabas says in chapter 6: *Why then milk and honey? Because the infant is first made alive with honey, and then with milk.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, the same blood and milk are symbols of the Lord's suffering and his doctrine. It is allowed for each of us who are children to boast in the Lord and say:

->*I boast to be of a good father and of such blood.*<-

It is now evident that milk is made from blood through change. We can observe this in cattle and oxen. In the spring time, when the air is more moist and the grass is more succulent, animals are first filled with blood. This can be known from the swelling of the veins. From this blood, milk is <margin>B</margin> poured out more richly. In the summer, however, the blood is dried by the heat and stops its transformation, so less is milked. Indeed, milk has a very natural connection with water, just as the spiritual washing has with spiritual food. Those who swallow a little cold with the milk are helped. The water prevents the milk from souring, not by conflict, but by ripening it through an inward connection. The same fellowship the Word has with baptism, milk has with water. This is the only liquid that mixes with water for the purpose of purifying, just as baptism is for the remission of sins. It is also <margin>C</margin> aptly mixed with honey for purification along with sweet food. The Word, mixed with kindness, heals the affections of the soul and clears away sins. The line:

> .... *Speech flows sweeter than honey*,

seems to me to be said of the Word, who is honey. In many places, prophecy exalts him *above honey and the honeycomb* <margin>Psalm 18:11; 118:103</margin>. Moreover, milk is also mixed...

---

*The infant is first given life with honey, then with milk.* Callimachus, in his *Hymn to Jupiter*, line 48:
<margin>D</margin>
> ... you sucked the rich breast 
> of the goat Amalthea, and ate sweet honeycomb besides.

Since baptism was a second birth, they gave the baptized honey mixed with milk to taste after the washing, as if they were tender infants. Compare Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 4; Third Council of Carthage, canon 24.
(48) **Honey.** Homer, *Iliad* 1, line 248, says of Nestor:
> ... the clear-voiced orator of the Pylians, 
> from whose tongue speech flowed sweeter than honey.
(49) **Milk and wine.** Jerome notes on Isaiah 55:1 that the Western Churches gave wine and milk to the newly baptized.

He also discusses the early Christian liturgical practice of giving honey and milk to the newly baptized to symbolize their rebirth as spiritual infants.</summary>
